summary: This informational document lists requirements for providing Diameter security at the level of individual Attribute-Value Pairs, for nodes that are not direct neighbors. It describes scenarios where hop-by-hop protection is not enough, and what an AVP-level solution would need to do.

eli5.summary: If a letter passes through several offices, each office could read it. This lists what is needed so only the right readers can see or trust particular pieces of the letter.

subtitle: End-to-end security for individual data elements in Diameter messages.

tldr.problem: Diameter protocol protects data only between neighboring nodes, but messages pass through intermediaries that should not see or modify certain fields intended for distant nodes.
tldr.mechanism: The specification requires mechanisms to protect individual Attribute-Value Pairs (AVPs) end-to-end, from their source to their intended recipient, using cryptographic protection.
tldr.outcome: Provides a framework for securing sensitive data in roaming and AAA broker networks, enabling protection against eavesdropping, manipulation, and impersonation.

facts.label: Diameter security mechanism
facts.value: Hop-by-hop TLS, DTLS, or IPsec between neighbors

facts.label: Gap addressed
facts.value: End-to-end protection of individual fields across multiple hops

today: RFC 7966 is an Informational specification of requirements, not a complete protocol. It documents what a solution must provide but does not define the actual mechanism. The document remains a reference for ongoing work on Diameter AVP-level security and for understanding the security challenges in federated AAA systems.

sections.title: The Problem: Hop-by-Hop vs. End-to-End
sections.content:
The Diameter base protocol defines security protection between neighboring Diameter nodes (direct peers) using TLS, DTLS, or IPsec. This hop-by-hop approach works well between two adjacent nodes but breaks down in networks where messages travel through multiple intermediaries.

In cellular networks and other AAA (Authentication, Authorization, Accounting) systems, a user's authentication request travels from a visited network through intermediary proxy servers (AAA brokers) to the home network. Hop-by-hop protection means each link is secured, but intermediaries can see and potentially modify sensitive data fields like cryptographic keys or user credentials. This document specifies requirements for protecting individual data elements end-to-end, from source to intended destination, regardless of intermediaries.
sections.eli5: Today, when a message travels through multiple stops, each stop can read everything. We need to protect certain pieces so only the right destination can read them.

sections.title: Security Threats
sections.content:
Eavesdropping occurs when intermediaries read sensitive data not intended for them. For example, an EAP-Master-Session-Key (a cryptographic key sent between server and client for wireless security) should not be readable by intermediaries in an AAA broker network.

Injection and Manipulation happen when compromised or misconfigured Diameter nodes insert, modify, or delete fields in messages. Adding extra charges, modifying quality-of-service parameters, or removing access restrictions could all occur at intermediary nodes.

Impersonation occurs when a message falsely claims to originate from a different domain than it actually does. An intermediary could alter fields to make data appear to come from a trusted source, enabling financial fraud or service disruption.

Without protection at the data-element level, networks must rely on strong edge verification and trust all intermediaries, which is difficult in federated AAA systems spanning multiple organizations.
sections.eli5: Bad things that happen: intermediaries can read secrets, they can change the message, or they can pretend messages came from someone else.

sections.title: Deployment Scenarios
sections.content:
The specification covers four scenarios for applying protection:

End-to-End Protection: A Diameter client and server apply protection to sensitive AVPs, allowing them to pass through intermediaries without being readable or modifiable. Both client and server must be updated to support this.

Middle-to-End Protection: A Diameter proxy near the client applies protection on behalf of clients within its domain, encrypting and signing AVPs before they leave the domain. The server receives protected data. Useful when clients cannot be updated.

End-to-Middle Protection: A Diameter proxy near the server verifies incoming protected AVPs. The client sends protected data; a proxy near the server removes the protection before forwarding to the server. Useful when servers cannot be updated.

Middle-to-Middle Protection: Security-enabled proxies at both ends apply and verify protection, leaving client and server unchanged. This is the most deployable scenario because it does not require modifying existing client and server infrastructure, only adding or updating proxies.
sections.eli5: Protection can happen in four ways: between the original sender and final receiver, from a proxy to the receiver, from the sender to a proxy, or between two proxies. The last way bothers existing equipment the least.

sections.title: Requirements for a Solution
sections.content:
A solution MUST support an extensible set of cryptographic algorithms so it can adapt as cryptography evolves, including modular updates without disrupting deployments.

It MUST support confidentiality, integrity, and data-origin authentication, working in a backwards-compatible way with legacy Diameter proxies that do not understand the protection. Some AVPs must not be confidentiality-protected but may be integrity-protected, such as routing AVPs that intermediaries need to read.

It MUST support replay protection to prevent attackers from replaying captured protected messages.

It MUST allow delegating security functionality to a proxy, so a proxy can protect AVPs on behalf of all clients in its domain, enabling incremental deployment.

It MUST support selective protection of specific AVPs, since some AVPs may be added, removed, or modified by intermediaries by design.

It MUST define mandatory-to-implement cryptographic algorithms for interoperability. It MUST support both symmetric and asymmetric keys (symmetric for speed, asymmetric for non-repudiation). Finally, it MUST include dynamic key management, reusing existing key management protocols if possible.
sections.eli5: A solution must use modern crypto, protect secrets and signatures, prevent replay attacks, let proxies protect data for clients, protect only certain fields, have a default algorithm, support both fast and secure key types, and handle changing keys over time.
